cards.back: A mathematical sentence that compares two expressions using <, >, ≤, or ≥. Example: $ x + 5 > 8 $.
[[imp:Less than or equal to]]. The value on the left is smaller than or equal to the value on the right. Key phrases: 'at most', 'no more than'.
[[imp:Greater than or equal to]]. The value on the left is larger than or equal to the value on the right. Key phrases: 'at least', 'no less than'.

cards.front: Translate into an inequality: 'A number w minus 3.5 is less than or equal to −2'.
Translate into an inequality: 'Three is less than a number n plus 5'.
cards.back: $ 3 < n + 5 $, which is equivalent to $ n + 5 > 3 $.
A value that makes the inequality true when substituted for the variable. An inequality can have many solutions.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:solution of an inequality]]?

cards.back: The set of all solutions of an inequality. For $ x > 2 $, the solution set includes every number greater than 2.
Use an open circle for < or >, when the boundary number is [[imp:NOT part of the solution]].
cards.front: When graphing an inequality, when do you use an [[imp:open circle]]?

cards.back: Use a closed circle for ≤ or ≥, when the boundary number [[imp:IS part of the solution]].
cards.front: When do you use a [[imp:closed circle]] on a number line graph?
How would you graph $ x > 2 $ on a number line?
cards.back: Draw an open circle at 2, then shade to the right, because all numbers greater than 2 are solutions.
Draw a closed circle at -3, then shade to the left, because all numbers less than or equal to -3 are solutions.
$ h \ge 48 $. The closed circle means 'greater than or equal to', and right shading means greater numbers.
cards.front: Write an inequality from this graph: closed circle at 48, shading to the right.

cards.back: $ p \le 600 $. 'Maximum' means the number cannot exceed 600, so at most 600.
cards.front: A sign says 'Maximum Capacity: 600'. Write an inequality for the number of people p that can be inside.
